hook.text: An oak is more than a tree: its leaves, bark, branches and acorns help make a home for woodland life.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

intro.text: English oak, also called pedunculate oak, grows into a broad-crowned deciduous tree. Its rounded, lobed leaves sit on very short stalks, while the acorns hang on much longer ones.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

intro.text: Each spring, catkins release pollen. By autumn, green acorns have ripened brown and become food for jays, squirrels and other animals.

source.label: Woodland Trust — Oak trees and wildlife

intro.text: A mature oak offers far more than shade: insects use its leaves and bark, birds nest in its cavities, and fungi and invertebrates live among its fallen leaves.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

claims.text: Oak bears male and female flowers on the same tree. Male catkins appear in April to May in Britain and release pollen into the wind.

source.label: Woodland Trust — Oak trees and wildlife

claims.text: Following pollination, acorns form, turn from green to brown and fall in autumn.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

claims.text: Caterpillars and other insects feed on oak leaves; birds and mammals eat its acorns. Mosses, lichens and fungi can occupy its bark, branches and the ground beneath.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

claims.text: When a jay buries acorns and leaves some behind, those seeds have a chance to grow into new trees.

source.label: Woodland Trust — Oak trees and wildlife

claims.text: Kew records the native range of Quercus robur from Europe eastwards to Iran, including Norway and Great Britain.

source.label: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

claims.text: This oak grows in deciduous woodland, and is especially familiar in woods, parks and hedgerows in Britain.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

claims.text: Acute and chronic oak decline are serious problems affecting oaks in Britain. Local impacts must not be presented as a uniform global trend.

source.label: Woodland Trust — English oak

claims.text: The oak processionary moth damages foliage in areas of England where it has established; this is a documented regional issue, not a global status statement.
